extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of history, religion, and intellectual history (scholars and educated general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarising the criteria, evidential practices, and intellectual causes that historical actors used to accept or reject miracles in antiquity and the early Christian centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of miracle (perpetual Divine interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perpetual interference of the Deity with the natural course of events is the earliest and simplest notion of miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the basic conceptual standard historically applied to label an event 'miraculous'—i.e., an event explained by direct supernatural intervention rather than natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of credulity: ignorance and defective inductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in miracles often arose 'in part from an ignorance of the laws of nature, and in part also from an incapacity for inductive reasoning, which led men merely to collect facts coinciding with their preconceived opinions, without attending to those that were inconsistent with them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing miracle-claims, consider whether observers lacked knowledge of natural laws or the habit of weighing contrary evidence; selection of confirming instances and ignoring disconfirming facts is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of selection bias and coincidence as apparent cumulative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence establishing these miracles is cumulative, and it is immeasurably greater than the evidence of many natural facts... there is no superstition that could not be defended by collecting coinciding facts; occasional verifications more than outweigh all the instances of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large volumes of anecdotal or clustered instances do not by themselves establish supernatural causation because coincidences and selective reporting can produce the appearance of cumulative proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional or juridical verification as historical standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The reality of the witch miracles was established by a critical tribunal... by the judicial decisions of the law courts of every European country, supported by the unanimous voice of public opinion, and corroborated by investigation of some of the ablest men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, official endorsement (courts, councils, universities, privy councils) functioned as a quality/authority metric for miracles; modern critique warns that institutional validation can nonetheless be mistaken or socially driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public experiments and authoritative demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that the king's touch can cure scrofula flourished... It was unshaken by the most numerous and public experiments. It was asserted by the privy council, by the bishops... by the University of Oxford, and by the enthusiastic assent of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public experiments and formal demonstrations were treated as strong evidence historically, but the text notes that such widespread public demonstrations did not guarantee truth—experiments can be flawed by social factors or methodological defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual-context test: persistence or cessation with changing intellectual conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: We disbelieve the miracles, because an overwhelming experience proves that in certain intellectual conditions, and under the influence of certain errors... superstitions invariably appear and flourish, and that, when these intellectual conditions have passed, the prodigies as invariably cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether purported miracles persist independently of prevailing intellectual or cultural conditions. If reports vanish as knowledge or critical habits spread, that is a diagnostic sign they may have been products of those conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exorcism as a special evidential category (demons won't expel demons)
rubrics_metrics.description: In one respect, it was observed, the miracle of exorcism was especially available for evidential purposes; for, as dæmons would not expel dæmons, it was the only miracle which was necessarily divine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, exorcism was treated as more probative than other wonders because of the claimed impossibility of a demon expelling another. Modern scrutiny questions this (e.g., mental illness, leading questions, staged performances), but this was an explicit historical criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and provenance of prophetic texts/oracles required for evidential use
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophecies forged by the Christians, and attributed by them to the heathen Sibyls, were accepted as genuine by the entire Church... but later critics demonstrated interpolations and forgeries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prophecy or oracular texts are used as evidence, their date, authorship, and textual integrity must be critically examined; forged or interpolated prophecies undermine evidential value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary vs. historical miracles: audience and purpose affect evidential weight
rubrics_metrics.description: With the exception of one or two isolated miracles... these prodigies, whether true or false, were wrought for the exclusive edification of confirmed believers... contemporary wonders were very unimpressive as general evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish miracles intended for 'edification of believers' from public, independent signs. Private or internal-audience miracles carry less evidential weight for neutral inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural investigatory standards (testimony, depositions, public reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a miracle was reported, [Augustine] ordered that a special examination into its circumstances should be made, and that the depositions of the witnesses should be read publicly to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice included formal inquiry procedures (gathered depositions, public hearings). Such procedural documentation is a criterion for assessing the thoroughness of historical miracle-investigation, but completeness and impartiality of procedure must be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural explanation and scientific prediction reduce credibility of supernatural accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Eclipses were supposed by the populace to foreshadow calamity; but the Roman soldiers believed they could beat drums to restore brightness... Pliny recounts astronomers' triumph in predicting and explaining eclipses and urges them to pursue their labour in breaking the thraldom of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful natural explanations and the development of predictive natural science diminish the need to invoke miracles; where natural law provides a reliable account, supernatural explanations are less credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptom equivalence and medical/psychological interpretations (possession vs disease)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern criticism has noted... that the symptoms of possession were for the most part identical with those of lunacy or epilepsy; that the excitement of an imposing religious ceremony might produce or suspend the disorder; that leading questions might be followed by desired answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether purported supernatural phenomena have plausible medical or psychological explanations, and whether social/ritual contexts could produce or shape the reported phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of relics and cures to imposture and social manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that they were genuine relics, the bones were brought in contact with a blind man, who was restored to sight... the Arians declared that the pretended demoniacs had been bribed by the saint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical signs (relics, cures) used as evidence must be evaluated for possible fraud, bribery, or performative staging; the mere association of relics with cures is insufficient without scrutiny of motives and controls.
